simple.meaning: כִּבְשָׂה (kibsâh) is a Hebrew concept word meaning “a ewe.” BibleIQ follows how Scripture develops this idea across its occurrences.
simple.biblicalBackground: The concept appears 8 times across Genesis, Leviticus, Numbers, 2 Samuel, beginning at Genesis 21:28. Its contexts include family line, flock, offering.
simple.inThisVerse: In this verse, the tapped English word is source-aligned to כִּבְשָׂה (H3535).
simple.whyItMatters: Concept words shape biblical themes. BibleIQ keeps the concept grounded in actual verse evidence instead of starting with a later theological definition.
simple.summary: כִּבְשָׂה (kibsâh) / H3535 is traced through Genesis 21:28, Genesis 21:29, Genesis 21:30, Leviticus 14:10 as a generated source-based concept entry.

definitions.full: H3535. kibsah or kabsah כַּבְשָׂה כִּבְשָׂה, noun feminine ewe-lamb ; ׳כִּ 2Sam 12:3 , 6 ; ׳כַּ Lev 14:10 ; Num 6:14 ; construct כִּבְשַׂת 2Sam 12:4 ; plural כְּבָשׂת Gen 21:29-30 , construct כִּבְשׂת 21:28 ; — ewe-lambs (7) set in witness 21:28-29 , 30 (E); used in sacrifice Lev 14:10 (purification), Num 6:14 (Nazirite; both P, and both || כָּבֶשׂ ); for food, in Nathan's parable 2Sam 12:3-4 , 6 .

occurrences.englishText: Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock by themselves.
Abimelech said to Abraham, “What do these seven ewe lambs, which you have set by themselves, mean?”
He said, “You shall take these seven ewe lambs from my hand, that it may be a witness to me, that I have dug this well.”

“On the eighth day he shall take two male lambs without defect, one ewe lamb a year old without defect, three tenths of an ephah* 1 ephah is about 22 liters or about 2/3 of a bushel of fine flour for a meal offering, mixed with oil, and one log† a log is a liquid measure of about 300 ml or 10 ounces of oil.

and he shall offer his offering to Yahweh: one male lamb a year old without defect for a burnt offering, one ewe lamb a year old without defect for a sin offering, one ram without defect for peace offerings,

but the poor man had nothing, except one little ewe lamb, which he had bought and raised. It grew up together with him, and with his children. It ate of his own food, drank of his own cup, and lay in his bosom, and was like a daughter to him.

A traveler came to the rich man, and he spared to take of his own flock and of his own herd, to prepare for the wayfaring man who had come to him, but took the poor man’s lamb, and prepared it for the man who had come to him.”
He must restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity!”
